name: Courts of Love and Notable Artisans (Libellus Sanguinis II Lore)

text.content: Founded by Eleanor of Aquitaine, the Courts of Love are among the @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.clans.JournalEntry.GaCuLGcjZZjf2EO6]{Toreador}'s proudest institutions: sheltered gatherings where noble ladies and knights play out elaborate games of courtship, giving rise to the romantic image of questing knights and unattainable ladies that @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.clans.JournalEntry.GaCuLGcjZZjf2EO6]{Toreador} troubadours make their livelihood singing about. A single Queen of Love, usually chosen by consensus, presides over each court, sets its rules, judges its suitors, and instructs its newest and least experienced members. A knight sets his heart on a lady and pursues her favor through deeds, patience, and public restraint rather than open declaration; the lady may accept or refuse him with little loss of face, though a lady who proves too capricious risks losing allies rather than gaining them. Beneath the courtly veneer, the game is thoroughly political — matches are arranged, suitors encouraged or discouraged, troubadours set loose on rivals, and unhappy marriages exploited for information, blackmail, or bloodlines useful to the @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.clans.JournalEntry.GaCuLGcjZZjf2EO6]{Toreador}'s schemes. Lady Isouda de Blaise presides over one such court, smaller than the famous courts of Aquitaine and Flanders, but disproportionately influential thanks to the high price — in gold, favors, and sometimes a rival clan's goodwill — she exacts from those eager to join it.

pages.name: Chivalry and the Cainite Knightly Orders

text.content: Chivalry has grown so entwined with the Courts of Love that a number of @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.clans.JournalEntry.GaCuLGcjZZjf2EO6]{Toreador} knights now treat it as a Via unto itself, holding to a Cainite Code of Chivalry (attributed, with some skepticism, to one Aloyius D'Etienne and rumored to be adapted from a much older source) that demands honor, fair dealing, and the protection of the weak, though its finer points are endlessly reinterpreted to suit whichever faction is currently citing it. Several @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.clans.JournalEntry.GaCuLGcjZZjf2EO6]{Toreador}-founded knightly orders uphold the code in practice. The White Company models itself on Galahad and Parsifal, binding its members to strict vows of honor, obedience, and celibacy toward Cainite women, and deals swiftly and permanently with oathbreakers. The Fellowship of Our Lady, numbering at most nine knights under the leadership of William Grey (who claims a vision of the Virgin charged him with protecting women), refuses to feed from women except in direst need; a recent quarrel with a @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.clans.JournalEntry.OpCOs3PLjmtl0QVu]{Ventrue} prince of Avignon has left the Fellowship under suspicion of heresy. The Order of Chanticleer hunts the @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.clans.JournalEntry.522046f606404b2b]{Baali} under the sign of a rising sun, its members' zeal and piety winning them few friends and leaving them caught between their mandate and the decadence of the @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.clans.JournalEntry.GaCuLGcjZZjf2EO6]{Toreador} elders they sometimes must confront.

pages.name: Simon of Malta, Keeper of the Cave Library

text.content: The greatest of the secret Cainite libraries preserving the classical world's learning from the wreck of the Roman Empire is a multi-chambered cave on Malta, tended by a @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.clans.JournalEntry.GaCuLGcjZZjf2EO6]{Toreador} who gives only the name Simon (or, in rare signed correspondence, "ben-Jacob"). Speculation holds he was Embraced somewhere in the Middle East during the Roman occupation, perhaps as early as the time of Christ, and was well educated for his era. His cavern holds chambers of Greek and Roman histories and poetry, inscriptions some claim are written in Enochian, Arabic literature and law, Druidic glyphs, a locked room of Hebrew and Aramaic texts, and a warded chamber of occult lore, demonology, and manuals of torture and war; one chamber, sealed behind a stone carved with a cedar tree, has never been opened even by Simon himself, and he refuses all offers to excavate it. Simon receives visitors only on urgent business, keeps his location shielded by a mortal knightly order headquartered on Malta, and has in recent years taken an interest in shaping the curricula of the new universities through mortal proxies supplied with copies of his texts — a project he seems to pursue with something between scholarly pride and a very old, very private grudge. A @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.clans.JournalEntry.OpCOs3PLjmtl0QVu]{Ventrue} who once destroyed a prized Hebrew parchment in front of him is said to flinch at the mere mention of Simon's name, and no one outside the two of them knows why.

vtmlarp.source: Libellus Sanguinis II: Keepers of the Word, Book One: Artisans (Toreador)
